promptText: Some argue governments should ban private cars in city centres to reduce pollution. Others believe individuals should have the right to drive wherever they wish. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

phases.correct: Government control over the use of privately owned cars in city centres.
distractors: The removal of all fossil fuel use from the whole world economy.
The comparison between public transport and the private motor car.
The redesign of crowded cities to remove their daily traffic jams.

phases.correct: The urgent need to reduce the pollution that city traffic creates.
distractors: The removal of every single source of pollution from all cities.
The building of wider main roads to ease the heavy congestion.
The creation of safer routes for people who walk or cycle.

phases.correct: cutting the exhaust fumes that people breathe in crowded city districts
distractors: banning all petrol and diesel engines inside the marked city districts
making car ownership a criminal offence for anyone living in a centre
forcing every commuter to walk or cycle to their place of work

phases.correct: Bans on petrol and diesel engines in marked central districts.
distractors: National targets that force every region to halve its carbon output by 2040.
The removal of inner-city roads to create parks and public squares.
The free supply of bicycles to every registered resident of a city.

phases.correct: a full ban creates problems for workers with no good bus or train service
distractors: traffic problems move to the roads just outside the banned city centre
the fall in emissions would be cancelled out within ten years by rising lorry traffic
exhaust fumes remain the greatest single threat to public health in cities

phases.correct: The freedom of each person to move around and travel as they choose.
distractors: The right of citizens to travel freely between one country and another.
The continued profit of the country's car manufacturing industry.
The convenience of the family car for households with several young children.

phases.correct: protecting the right of people to cross the city without state interference
distractors: protecting the earnings of families whose work depends on driving into the centre daily
letting drivers ignore environmental rules whenever they happen to be short of time
promising every motorist a free parking space somewhere in the city centre

phases.correct: Free entry to central districts along the ordinary public road network.
distractors: Congestion charges placed on every vehicle that enters the central zone.
Multi-storey car parks built on every block of the central shopping district.
The withdrawal of bus services so that residents are forced to drive.

phases.correct: unlimited driving builds up into constant traffic jams and dirty air
distractors: unrestricted driving always destroys the quality of life in every city
private motoring is already too expensive for most households in the city
people who drive everywhere tend to develop heart problems later in their lives

phases.correct: councils should invest in public transport while phasing out the dirtiest vehicles
distractors: every country must ban the private motor car outright if urban air quality is to improve
governments should ban private cars and leave citizens to make their own arrangements
the right to drive should be absolute as long as motorists pay a pollution charge

phases.correct: good city policy has to protect the environment and keep people able to travel
distractors: cleaner air is the single most important aim of government policy everywhere
public transport always costs the daily commuter far less than running a private car
citizens will never give up the convenience of the private car of their own accord

promptText: Some say governments should fund only university science degrees because they are the most useful. Others believe public money should continue to support arts subjects. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

phases.correct: The way the state divides its funding between university subjects.
distractors: The total amount of money that a government spends on its education system.
The rising tuition fees that today's university students have to pay.
The difficulty of persuading school leavers to enter the technical fields.

phases.correct: The priority given to science subjects in order to drive new technology.
distractors: The belief that only scientific study is of any value to society.
The transfer of all humanities funding to laboratory-based university departments.
The high cost of building and maintaining well-equipped research laboratories.

phases.correct: directing money into subjects that produce a measurable return for industry
distractors: paying the full cost of degrees in medicine, engineering and applied physics
requiring science graduates to work for the state that paid for their studies
doubling the tuition fees paid by students of the creative arts and humanities

phases.correct: Full state funding for degrees in medical research, software engineering and physics.
distractors: Government campaigns urging schoolchildren to take an interest in science.
Universities giving their newest buildings to the science departments alone.
Mathematics made a compulsory subject for every single undergraduate student.

phases.correct: a narrow focus on technical skill leaves out the moral judgement that new technology needs
distractors: a purely scientific course leaves graduates unable to reason about ethics at all
laboratory subjects already attract the larger share of private research investment
medical and engineering degrees lead directly into the jobs that industry needs

phases.correct: The continued use of public money to fund the humanities and creative subjects.
distractors: The public subsidy of orchestras, galleries and national theatre companies.
The duty of science students to study poetry before they may graduate.
The payment of a salary by the state to practising artists and musicians.

phases.correct: preserving culture and teaching students to communicate and analyse society
distractors: supporting the export earnings that national film, design and publishing industries create
making sure national museums buy enough new works to attract paying visitors
letting students choose the subjects that place them under the least pressure

phases.correct: Public grants for university courses in history, literature and modern languages.
distractors: State support for every artistic project that any citizen chooses to propose.
Free concert and theatre tickets handed out to every student enrolled at a university.
Large public sculptures commissioned for the centre of every major city.

phases.correct: funding the arts without limit can produce graduates the economy does not need
distractors: no humanities graduate can expect to find work in the field they studied
humanities departments are far cheaper to run than the scientific ones are
the reading of serious literature has fallen sharply since the arrival of the internet

phases.correct: the state should fund science generously while keeping targeted support for the arts
distractors: governments must fund every science subject and withdraw all support from the arts entirely
governments should fund science well and leave the arts to private donors
every degree should be funded equally because all knowledge is worth the same

phases.correct: a strong society needs both the ability to invent and the wisdom to guide invention
distractors: a nation's wealth depends mainly on the size of its total education budget
new technology is the only reliable route to lasting national wealth, power and influence
universities themselves are best placed to decide how their own funding is divided

promptText: Some believe prisons exist strictly to punish those who break the law. Others argue they should concentrate entirely on reforming offenders. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

phases.correct: The basic purpose that the modern prison system is meant to serve.
distractors: The way society responds to crime in each of its many different forms.
The social conditions that cause ordinary people to turn to crime.
The rising cost of housing offenders who have already been convicted.

phases.correct: The priority given to punishing those who break the country's laws.
distractors: The belief that punishment on its own can prevent all crime.
The deliberate decision to keep conditions inside prisons hard and bare.
The return of the death penalty for the most serious offences.

phases.correct: taking away an offender's freedom as the direct result of their own actions
distractors: handing fixed prison sentences to those who commit serious or repeated crimes
making inmates do unpaid work to repay the debt they owe to society
publishing every conviction widely so that possible offenders are shamed into obeying

phases.correct: Fixed prison sentences imposed for serious or repeated criminal offences.
distractors: Life imprisonment imposed for every offence that involves violence of any kind.
Long periods of solitary confinement for the most serious criminals.
The permanent removal of family visiting rights from all inmates.

phases.correct: a purely punitive system leads to high reoffending among prisoners once released
distractors: punishment can never change the way an offender behaves after release
the cost of keeping people in prison for many years falls upon the law-abiding taxpayer
offenders held under harsh regimes become more determined to escape from them

phases.correct: The priority given to rehabilitation and to changing how offenders think.
distractors: The prevention of crime through investment in the poorest communities.
The provision of comfortable living quarters for every single inmate.
The early release of prisoners who show sincere and lasting regret for their crimes.

phases.correct: giving inmates job training and therapy that deals with the causes of their offending
distractors: promising that no offender who receives therapy will ever return to crime
prescribing medication to offenders whose behaviour cannot be managed otherwise
keeping prisoners busy with organised sport so that idleness causes no trouble

phases.correct: Education classes inside prison together with counselling for drug and alcohol problems.
distractors: Job training that deals with the underlying causes of criminal offending.
Weekend home leave granted to prisoners who have behaved well inside.
Fully funded university degrees awarded to every prisoner serving a sentence.

phases.correct: a purely rehabilitative system denies victims justice and weakens the deterrent power of law
distractors: no victim will ever accept a sentence that concentrates only on reforming the offender
a system built only on punishment releases offenders ready to commit new crimes
offenders who complete job training reoffend at considerably lower rates

phases.correct: prisons should combine the loss of freedom with compulsory programmes that reform offenders
distractors: every prison must abandon punishment outright and devote itself entirely to reforming offenders
custodial sentences ought to be replaced by therapy programmes that offenders must attend
society should concentrate on preventing crime, which would make prisons largely unnecessary

phases.correct: protecting the public needs both the containment of danger and a fall in reoffending
distractors: a nation is judged in the end by how humane its social institutions are
imprisonment without limit creates a cost that no national treasury can realistically carry
every offender can be returned to society if given enough counselling and time

promptText: Many believe that working from home benefits employees and companies alike. Others think it isolates staff and lowers overall productivity. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

phases.correct: The move by many organisations towards remote and more flexible ways of working.
distractors: The reshaping of the world labour market by digital technology.
The falling commercial demand for office space in major cities.
The technologies that allow teams in different places to work together.

phases.correct: The benefit that remote work brings to employees and employers alike.
distractors: The universal advantage that remote arrangements bring to every single organisation.
The better balance between work and home life reported by home-based staff.
The duty of every firm to let its staff work away from the office.

phases.correct: removing travel time and office costs, which raises both freedom and efficiency
distractors: cutting the property costs employers carry and keeping staff for longer
letting staff decide their own working hours without any supervision from their managers
moving the cost of equipment and electricity from the employer to the employee

phases.correct: Scattered firms reporting lower property costs and better staff retention.
distractors: The nationwide fall in demand for commercial office space since 2020.
Companies moving their head offices into smaller and cheaper premises.
Staff joining departmental meetings by video from home several times each week.

phases.correct: remote work without structure removes the line between work and home and causes burnout
distractors: employees left to work at home without structure will always neglect the duties they have
remote arrangements give the employee back several unpaid hours of travel each week
home working suits only those jobs that can be carried out on a computer screen

phases.correct: The harm done to teamwork and to the mental wellbeing of staff.
distractors: The decline of city centre economies that depend on office workers.
The impossibility of carrying out most occupations anywhere outside a workplace.
The extra spending on home office furniture that employers must now cover.

phases.correct: removing casual contact between colleagues and breaking up the unity of working teams
distractors: slowing projects down through communication that never happens in real time
leaving organisations exposed to the failure of home internet connections
allowing staff to ignore instructions that they would never question inside a shared office

phases.correct: Projects delayed by staff isolation and by messages answered many hours later.
distractors: The complete collapse of new ideas in any firm whose staff never meet in person.
New recruits resigning within months of joining a scattered organisation.
Employees dealing with household duties during their paid working hours.

phases.correct: falling output usually reflects weak digital management rather than remote work itself
distractors: output across the whole national economy has not fallen since remote work spread
new employees learn far less about their work when they never sit beside an experienced colleague
the problem belongs to one generation and will disappear as the workforce changes

phases.correct: firms should adopt hybrid models that pair remote flexibility with purposeful meetings in person
distractors: no organisation can work effectively unless all of its employees work from home
employers ought to require office attendance in order to protect overall productivity
staff should decide each morning whether or not they will come to the workplace

phases.correct: a hybrid arrangement raises efficiency while protecting the wellbeing and creativity of staff
distractors: employers should combine home working with days set aside for meeting in the office
employees will resign in large numbers if forced into an office five days a week
the office has become an expensive relic of an older and more industrial age

promptText: Some parents firmly restrict their children's screen time to protect healthy development. Others insist digital devices are essential for modern learning and should not be limited. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

phases.correct: The control of how much digital technology children are exposed to.
distractors: The effect that digital technology has upon the population as a whole.
The age at which a child ought to be given their first smartphone.
The influence of social media upon the behaviour of teenagers.

phases.correct: The setting of firm limits in order to protect children's health and growth.
distractors: The removal of every electronic device from the family home entirely.
The damage that long hours of screen use do to developing eyesight.
The preference many parents have for books over electronic entertainment.

phases.correct: preventing inactive habits and limiting the effect of constant stimulation on young attention
distractors: banning the use of tablets on school days in favour of outdoor games and free play
supervising the material a child meets when using the internet alone at home
making sure that homework is finished before any device is allowed for entertainment

phases.correct: Household rules that ban all tablet use on school days in favour of outdoor play.
distractors: National guidelines limiting screen time for citizens of every age group.
The removal of every entertainment application from a child's telephone.
Schools banning computers from the classroom under all circumstances.

phases.correct: harsh restriction leaves children unable to use technology and cut off from friends
distractors: children raised without any devices are always excluded by their classmates
children who are denied devices at home will borrow them from classmates and neighbours
rules of this kind cause resentment and damage the relationship with parents

phases.correct: The place of free digital access in the education children receive today.
distractors: The dependence of the modern workplace upon digital communication tools.
The role of the tablet in occupying a child during a parent's working day.
The belief that educational software will one day replace the classroom teacher entirely.

phases.correct: giving young people confidence with technology and access to information worldwide
distractors: making certain that no child is ever placed at a disadvantage in the future labour market
letting pupils follow their own interests without constant direction from a teacher
teaching young people to repair and look after their own devices and equipment

phases.correct: Software that teaches coding or a language through games children want to play.
distractors: Parental controls limiting a child's tablet to educational applications only.
Video platforms on which children come across some occasional educational material.
Calculator applications that finish a pupil's mathematics homework for them.

phases.correct: access without guidance usually turns into passive watching rather than real learning
distractors: devices without supervision always destroy a child's ability to concentrate
few families can afford a separate device for each child in the household
strict limits leave a child unable to use the digital tools that their schooling assumes

phases.correct: parents should move from limiting screen time towards guiding its content and purpose
distractors: parents must remove screens from childhood altogether if children are to develop normally
screen time ought to be forbidden on weekdays and allowed freely at weekends
children should use computers under supervision at school but never at home

phases.correct: preparing children for a digital future means using its benefits without dependence
distractors: digital technology has now reshaped almost every part of modern economic life
technical skill has now become a requirement for almost every occupation and profession
children lose interest in screens as soon as other activities are offered to them

promptText: Some think international tourism strengthens the local economy. Others argue it erodes local cultures and harms the natural environment. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

phases.correct: The effects of foreign tourism on local economies and the environment.
distractors: The general growth of the worldwide travel industry over the past fifty years.
The reasons why people from wealthy countries choose to travel abroad.
The damage that large numbers of visitors do to famous historic sites.

phases.correct: The new money that foreign visitors bring into the local economy.
distractors: The belief that tourism can cure every problem a poor region has.
The jobs that hotels, restaurants and tour companies create for local young people.
The tax that national governments collect from international airlines.

phases.correct: bringing outside money into local businesses and paying for roads and schools
distractors: opening beach resorts that employ hundreds of workers from the nearby villages
persuading young local people to move abroad and send their wages home
forcing national governments to spend their own money on new airports and motorways

phases.correct: Coastal towns paying for clinics and schools with a small tourist tax.
distractors: National governments funding a whole health service from the tax on air travel.
Villages beside a national park selling their land to foreign hotel chains.
Airlines adding extra flights to popular islands during the summer season.

phases.correct: most of the profit returns to the foreign firms that own the hotels and airlines
distractors: local communities never see any share of the money that foreign visitors spend
visitor spending has become the largest single source of income in many regions

phases.correct: The damage that visitors do to local traditions and to fragile natural places.
distractors: The harm that air travel does to the global climate as a whole.
The rise in house prices that pushes young families out of the area.
The rudeness of some foreign visitors towards the people who serve them.

phases.correct: turning real traditions into shows for sale and using up scarce water and land
distractors: destroying every local custom and every natural habitat in the whole region

phases.correct: Dying coral reefs and old quarters turned into rows of souvenir shops.
distractors: Ancient monuments closed to the public because of the damage crowds cause.

Airports made larger so that bigger aircraft can land on a small island.

phases.correct: visitor money often pays for the very parks and buildings that need protecting
distractors: tourism always saves far more of the natural world than it ever destroys

phases.correct: governments should limit visitor numbers and spend tourist money on culture and nature
distractors: every country should close its most famous sites to visitors until the damage is repaired

foreign travel should be discouraged so that people spend their holidays at home

phases.correct: a place that sells its character will lose the very thing visitors come for

promptText: Some argue that government spending on space is wasteful and should be redirected to problems on Earth. Others believe space research delivers vital technological progress. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

phases.correct: The value of spending public money on the exploration of outer space.

phases.correct: The case for moving space budgets towards more urgent human needs.
distractors: The demand that all scientific research stop until poverty has ended.

The wish of taxpayers to see their money spent inside their own country.

phases.correct: moving limited public money to urgent problems such as poverty and disease
distractors: closing the national space agency and giving its buildings to local universities
asking wealthy private companies to pay for the cost of space missions instead

phases.correct: Governments moving space funding into housing and the fight against disease.
distractors: International agreements that force every nation to cut its research budget by half.

phases.correct: space budgets are a very small part of spending, so cutting them would change little

phases.correct: The useful technology that long-term research into space produces.
distractors: The national pride that a successful space mission brings to a country.

The profits that private firms earn by launching satellites for other countries.

phases.correct: forcing new inventions under hard conditions, which later move into everyday use
distractors: producing every important invention of the last fifty years through work on space missions

phases.correct: Satellite navigation, water cleaning systems and medical scanners that began as space research.
distractors: Rockets that can now carry paying tourists on short flights above the atmosphere.

phases.correct: the same inventions might have been made more cheaply by research aimed directly at them
distractors: no useful technology has ever come out of any government space programme

phases.correct: governments should keep a small, carefully aimed space programme while most money meets social needs
distractors: all space funding should stop until every country has solved its social problems
space research should be left entirely to private companies and wealthy investors

phases.correct: helping people now and building knowledge for the future are not opposing aims

phases.correct: choice only means something when a cheap and healthy option is actually available nearby

promptText: Some believe printed newspapers will be completely replaced by online news. Others argue that print media will always keep a valued place in society. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
